title: AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities
content:
On October 9, 2026, four researchers posted a paper titled “AI Models Can Provably Hide Arbitrary Capabilities” on arXiv. The authors note there that it has been accepted at NeurIPS 2026. They hid a second, encrypted neural network inside an AI model’s weights, one that runs only when the input contains a secret trigger. In their tests, neither fine-tuning (further training on a specific task) nor adding noise to the weights brought it out.
That matters wherever an open model runs on a local computer or a vendor delivers a retrained model. Testing a model shows what it can do. But as the paper points out, an audit that finds nothing doesn’t prove a capability is absent. In October 2026, an Anthropic model even wondered mid-reasoning whether it was in a test environment, right after it cracked the mystery of the NSA-supplied NIST curve seeds.
An encrypted locker inside the model’s weights
The authors are Andis Draguns (Contramont Research), Sumeet Ramesh Motwani and Christian Schroeder de Witt (University of Oxford), and Raymond Douglas (ACS Research). Their threat model is an attacker who tampers with a model’s weights before deployment, such as a malicious insider or a compromised supply chain. The paper’s hypothetical example is a coding assistant that also carries a hacking model, set to switch on when it spots signs it has been deployed in critical infrastructure. The auditor, meanwhile, gets the full model, weights included, and can throw any method at it.
The core building block is what cryptographers call a digital locker. The secret key is run through a hash function (here, the Keccak family that underpins the SHA-3 standard), and the output is combined with the content to be protected. With the right key, the computation recovers the content; any other key yields meaningless bits, and the locker reports failure. The mechanism is in plain view, but without the key, and under standard cryptographic assumptions, nobody can open it, recover the key or tell what’s inside.
The researchers put a small neural network’s weights inside that locker, then compile the whole thing into the kind of computational blocks today’s language models are built from. Every time the host model processes an input, it tries to open the locker with it. With the trigger, the hidden capability runs. Without it, the model behaves normally.
Retraining doesn’t unlock the encrypted model
The hidden capability is a small classifier: given reagents and a candidate product, it predicts whether the reaction yields that product. The authors picked it as a stand-in for a capability tied to chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear risks, and kept it to classification to avoid direct misuse. Their baseline is the standard technique, a “password-locked” model trained to answer correctly only when the prompt includes a password.
After 500 steps of supervised fine-tuning on the task itself, the password-locked model hits 92.8% accuracy. The encrypted model stays at 50.9%, essentially a coin flip, and a control model whose locker holds a random network scores 50.6%.
Accuracy on test data, averaged over three runs (Table 2 in the paper):
Adding noise of 0.01 or 0.1 to the weights before retraining doesn’t materially change these results. An automated trigger search finds an 8-bit key by trying all 256 possible values, doing no better than a random search. With a 16-bit key, it stays at 52.7% within its search budget. With the correct trigger, the encrypted model trails (73.5% versus 92.7%) because it uses a different, smaller classifier that fits inside the host.
A full-strength cryptographic version, produced by an optimizing mode of the authors’ compiler, uses a 128-bit key and 24 rounds of Keccak. The resulting model has 110 layers and 3.58 billion parameters, counting zeros. Given the right key, it reproduces the classifier on all the test data, and across the 10,000 wrong keys tested, it behaves normally.
Telltale signs in the weights
The paper doesn’t claim the circuit is invisible. The raw compiled weights are easy to spot: about 99% are exactly zero and most of the rest are whole numbers, nothing like a normally trained model. The authors tested a disguise that brings these statistics close to those of a freshly initialized model, but they report unusual correlations between weights in the same layer, which could give the construction away.
With a long enough key, the guarantee still protects the key and the content, and spotting the anomaly doesn’t change that. According to the authors, an auditor may not be able to tell whether an odd structure hides a dangerous capability, a harmless watermark or a technical artifact, or remove it without damaging the model. That leaves an expensive option: not using the model at all.
Who is exposed?
Claude or ChatGPT subscribers never get the weights and can’t audit those models anyway. Their protection is trust in the provider and its own safeguards.
The exposure starts with handling the weights directly: an open model downloaded from Hugging Face, an “improved” version posted by an unknown account, or a model retrained by a vendor. The authors say the threat applies wherever a model is deployed in a high-stakes setting without a full record of how it was trained. Our article on the AI worms Anthropic described covers other risks of open-weight models.
France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, flagged this risk in its security recommendations for a generative AI system, published April 29, 2024: an untrusted third party can train a model to respond differently when it receives a certain request. It offered two remedies: audit the model, or keep it out of critical applications. The new paper shows that testing-based audits have a fundamental limit against a determined attacker.
According to the authors, the risk scales with the hidden capability and with how much authority the host model has. An agent that sends emails or places orders has far more of it than a tool that summarizes documents on a standalone computer. Understanding how models work inside, known as interpretability, is one of the research areas Anthropic funds through its fellowship program (see our article on that paid research program).
A costly proof of concept
The demo hides a classifier with 672 weights, and each hidden weight adds about 3.1 million parameters to the host model, counting zeros. The experimental model has 38 layers and about 2.07 billion parameters, only 1.9 million of them nonzero; the authors present these as proof-of-concept costs. The full construction hasn’t been built into a real pretrained model yet. Only individual building blocks have been tested inside Gemma 3 270M, a small Google model.
Building one takes expertise in both cryptography and machine learning, and the authors don’t claim such circuits emerge on their own in ordinary training. In their view, a small hidden circuit that boosts an already capable model, for fraud or sabotage, say, has yet to be demonstrated. They’re releasing their models so other teams can test defenses against them.
Defenses still being worked out
The authors think more sophisticated methods could still detect anomalies in the weights, disguise or not. They also see promise in monitoring a model while it runs, since a hidden capability might reveal itself when it executes. The paper adds a complementary defense: documenting a model’s full chain of custody, from data to training.

report.summary: Oxford-led researchers prove a model's weights can conceal an encrypted hidden capability that survives fine-tuning, weight noise and trigger searches, so clean audits no longer prove absence.
report.background: Open-weight models are now downloaded, fine-tuned and redistributed constantly — from Hugging Face repos to vendor-delivered retrained checkpoints — so whoever touches the weights before deployment can alter behaviour. Earlier work showed models could be trained to behave normally until a password appears (password-locked models) or a trigger date arrives (sleeper agents), but those behaviours were fragile: further training or trigger search could expose them. Meanwhile auditors rely on testing, red-teaming and probing to certify safety. France's ANSSI already warned in April 2024 that an untrusted third party could train a model to respond differently to a specific request, recommending either auditing the model or keeping it out of critical systems. This paper attacks the first remedy directly, moving the concealment problem from machine learning into cryptography, where the guarantees are much stronger.
key_points: The payload is a small neural network's weights placed inside a cryptographic 'digital locker': the secret key is hashed with Keccak (the SHA-3 primitive) and combined with the content. Anyone can see the mechanism, but without the key nothing is recoverable. The whole construction is compiled into ordinary transformer blocks, so every forward pass quietly attempts to open the locker; only the trigger input succeeds, and the host otherwise behaves normally.

Standard countermeasures fail. After 500 steps of supervised fine-tuning on the hidden task, a conventional password-locked model reaches 92.8% accuracy while the encrypted model sits at 50.9% — a coin flip. Adding noise of 0.01 or 0.1 to the weights changes nothing, and an automated trigger search over an 8-bit key does no better than random, staying near 52.7% at 16 bits within budget.

A full-strength build works exactly as designed: a 128-bit key with 24 Keccak rounds yields a 110-layer, 3.58-billion-parameter model that reproduces the hidden classifier perfectly on all test data with the right key and behaves normally across 10,000 wrong keys. The demonstration capability was a deliberately narrow chemistry classifier, chosen as a safe proxy for CB RN risk.

The concealment is not invisible. Roughly 99% of compiled weights are exactly zero and most others are whole numbers — nothing like a trained model. The authors' disguise brings summary statistics close to a fresh initialization, but unusual within-layer correlations remain. Crucially, spotting the anomaly does not break the cryptography: an auditor still cannot tell whether it hides a dangerous capability, a watermark or an artifact.

It is a costly proof of concept, not a turnkey attack. Each hidden weight adds about 3.1 million host parameters, the demo classifier has 672 weights, and only individual building blocks were tested inside Gemma 3 270M — not a real pretrained model. The authors say it requires expertise in both cryptography and machine learning, and do not claim such circuits arise spontaneously from ordinary training.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes model security from a detection problem into a supply-chain trust problem: an audit that finds nothing is now formally weak evidence, which undermines the certification practices vendors and regulators are building. Open-weight distribution is most exposed, since anyone can post an 'improved' checkpoint carrying a hidden circuit. For developers, the practical lesson is provenance over probing — prefer signed, chain-of-custody-tracked weights, and treat unfamiliar fine-tunes as untrusted code. For regular users of ChatGPT or Claude the risk is largely indirect, since weights never leave the provider; exposure arrives when a critical system silently runs a third-party local model. Expect the field to pivot toward runtime monitoring, since a hidden capability may betray itself only when it fires.
report.tools: To follow up: the authors' released experimental models and the arXiv paper (NeurIPS 2026), useful as test benches for defenses. For detection work, try Garak and the LLM-Attack/safety-scanner suites for behavioural probing, TransformerLens for weight-level inspection, and sparse autoencoder toolkits for interpretability. For supply-chain hygiene, watch Hugging Face model signing and provenance metadata, plus weight-statistic anomaly checks. Gemma 3 270M is the practical sandbox the authors used for component tests.
